Confidentiality protocols: Recognising the sensitivity of services like wellbeing and sexual health, the team utilised side doors to provide separate, discreet access to confidential spaces.

Integrated layouts: Designers linked individual rooms to the main hub space. This configuration allows new providers to engage more easily with existing youth club members, facilitating easier referral and connection to new services.

Shared infrastructure: The hub includes a hot-desk office for co-located staff, ensuring a dedicated workspace for partner organisations. Furthermore, a shared storage agreement allows various providers to access equipment, thereby increasing the range of activities available while simultaneously reducing costs for individual youth providers. The local authority will be added to the Youth database linking external commissioned services to youth monitoring data.

Operational coordination: While the local authority leads on central timetable setting—prioritising targeted clubs during popular time slots—the structure remains flexible. Delivery providers are encouraged to build relationships with youth workers and attendees during these sessions, fostering a dynamic, youth-led schedule that evolves based on participant needs and partner collaboration.

3.3. Workforce

The workforce within a Young Futures Hubs is likely to consist of a range of paid staff and volunteers, with different skills and competencies, qualification frameworks, and professional bodies. To help staff build essential competencies for their roles, hubs ought to deliver internal and external training along with peer learning opportunities. These programs should adapt to the evolving needs of young people while embedding key youth work principles into every role. Training should also be regularly reviewed using feedback from young people.

Essential:

The workforce will vary depending on the services offered and is typically multidisciplinary in make-up. However, the type of roles that you would expect to see include:

Partnership/Hub Coordinator

Lead Youth Worker with Level 6 qualification or equivalent experience

Mental Health Practitioner/counsellor, trained and registered to support triaging, and with crisis response as needed.

Careers and Opportunity Lead

Violence Prevention Lead

Safeguarding Lead

Volunteers, including young people.

Staff and volunteers are equipped and enabled to respond to young people’s needs, and deliver the services offered in the hub, with reflective practice embedded in the multi-disciplinary team.

All employers involved in Young Futures Hubs must follow the minimum recruitment practices in your code of practice, meaning a DBS check.

Staff should be capable of providing early help for common and emerging needs, including anxiety, low mood, emotional distress, trauma-related needs, neurodivergence-related support needs, and family or relationship difficulties. This may include brief assessment, developing a collaborative understanding of need, guided self-help, low-intensity psychological interventions, group work, counselling, peer support, family-informed work and advice for parents or carers.

Staff should be equipped with the skills to manage complex needs in an appropriate way, including needs that have already materialised but haven’t been fully identified such as vulnerability to exploitation, violence, abuse, debt, parent/carer imprisonment and family relationships. This should include staff training in trauma-informed and non-stigmatising practice, mental health first aid, safeguarding and cultural competence and neurodiversity support.

Staff are aware of wider local services available that may not be offered within the hub and can confidently link young people to them e.g. housing support, support for parental imprisonment.

Delivery must align with existing multi-agency safeguarding arrangements, recognising the legal duties of settings and ensuring strong operational links between hubs and safeguarding leads. Staff should understand local safeguarding pathways and wider safeguarding processes.

Evaluate current operational capabilities and align with professional standards for relevant roles to design and implement a targeted workforce training and development plan based on the insights gained.

Prioritise workforce stability to give staff time to build genuine, trusted relationships.

Hubs should ensure appropriate clinical supervision, consultation and escalation arrangements for staff delivering mental health support. This should include clear thresholds and escalation processes for when young people need specialist NHS mental health services, crisis support, safeguarding intervention or other statutory responses.

Go further:

Involve young people in the recruitment, induction and training of staff.

Ensure the workforce is relatable and reflective of the local community, including those with lived experiences similar to the young people they are supporting.

Provide opportunities for young people to be part of the hub workforce.

Create clear opportunities for youth leadership within the staff structure.

When developing a workforce training plan, encourage staff to undertake enhanced safeguarding training.

Helpful resources

NYA Safeguarding and Risk Management Hub

UK Youth Safe Spaces Framework

Provider framework on Mentoring

Safeguarding in out-of-school settings e-learning

National Information Centre on Children of Offenders

Youth Work Code of Ethics

4. Service delivery and referrals

4.1. Services

Young Futures Hubs should build on existing strengths while remaining flexible to meet emerging needs. Strong coordination across teams and partners will prevent duplication of services, align new developments with what already works, and create a more integrated and effective offer for young people.

1.3. Young people’s vision for Young Futures Hubs

Young people shared their vision for Young Futures Hubs through the Youth Transformation Task and Finish Group of 15 people aged 14 to 25 and over five pop-up consultation events across the country for younger participants (aged 10 to 14).

They told us they welcomed the ambition of Young Futures Hubs to create safe, accessible, community-based spaces where they can access support, pathways to growth and trusted adults. They highlighted that the success of Young Futures Hubs will depend less on buildings or services and more on whether hubs create meaningful relationships as “staff make or break the experience”, their hope for the hubs is that they feel genuinely welcoming and are shaped by the needs of local young people to feel like a “home away from home” rather than an institution.

Successful hubs should be a space where young people:

feel safe

feel welcome

feel understood

feel respected

feel represented

feel listened to

feel connected

feel able to influence decisions

1.4. Target cohort

Young Futures Hubs are open to all young people aged 10 to 18 (up to 25 for young people with SEND) with flexibility to change the age range according to local need. Within this open access approach, local authorities should prioritise engagement and support for young people showing early risk factors linked to poor outcomes in mental health, opportunity and crime (see table below). Evidence shows that early intervention delivered through trusted adults with welcoming, accessible provision is effective in preventing escalation and improving long-term outcomes.

Young Futures Hubs should provide non-stigmatising support that builds trust, strengthens resilience, and connects young people to the right help at the right time. While delivery should reflect local context and need, local authorities are expected to ensure that resources are focused on young people at risk of becoming Not in Education, Employment or Training (NEET), vulnerable to being drawn into crime, or developing poor mental health outcomes.

While anyone can access services, hubs should be particularly accessible and tailored toward those with early risk factors, with the aim for 60% of young people accessing Young Futures Hubs targeted services having one or more early risk factor(s).

The following list is not exhaustive and provides early indicators that young people may be at risk. This is to be used alongside practitioner insight and consideration of individual circumstances.

List of early risk indicators across programme objectives

Early risk indicators include:

being disengaged, excluded or absent from school/ not in education, employment or training

probable mental health condition

looked after/care-experience

harm-involved social networks

experience of poverty or deprivation

anti-social behaviour (perpetration of) or previous offending (particularly lower-level crimes such as stealing or minor theft)

having a special educational need or disability (SEND)

being in contact with social care, or parents/carers contacted by social or educational services about young persons’ behaviour

having a parent/carer or guardian with a disability or mental health condition (including substance misuse)

multiple Adverse Childhood Experiences[footnote 1]

Engagement with the target cohort should be achieved through three primary mechanisms:

Strategic hub placement: Establishing Young Futures Hubs within high-need geographic areas to ensure proximity to the target cohort, effectively creating a model of targeted open access.

Partner-led identification: Local authorities should use local data, insight, and the expertise of trained professionals and partners to identify, engage, and support these young people to access provision.

Strategic outreach and detached youth work: Young Futures Hubs should provide a targeted outreach and detached service for young people in spaces and areas that they feel most comfortable.

2. Guiding principles

Young Futures Hubs should be built on the core values of youth work that prioritise voluntary participation, personal empowerment, and positive relationships between young people and practitioners.

2.1. Young voices: experts by experience

Young people should be involved in decisions that directly affect them, including how services are delivered and when support is available.

Young Futures Hubs should:

empower young people to participate in decision-making

use the Lundy Model to ensure young people have:

space

voice

audience

influence

actively engage and empower underrepresented groups to share their views, including girls and young women, young people from minority ethnic backgrounds, young people with SEND, and care-experienced young people

2.2. Trusted relationships

Trusted relationships are central to effective early intervention. Young people must have access to consistent, non-judgemental support from adults they know and trust.

Young Futures Hubs should:

employ empathetic, skilled staff who reflect the communities they serve and take all perspectives into account

prioritise relationship-based practice across all provision

support warm handovers between services, particularly during transition points

create environments that promote belonging, peer support, and community connection

No young person should have to navigate support systems alone.

2.3. Equality, diversity and inclusion (EDI)

Young Futures Hubs must be inclusive, accessible, and welcoming to all young people. No young person should be excluded from support because of their background, identity, needs, or circumstances.
